post_details: Hi Everyone! Here is a quick video showing an easy method to make pleats! It's really easy to attached a small piece and then build, fold and simulate as you go. If you do your math correctly you can start with one little piece and add the pleat allowance using offset pattern outline. then you can merge the sections together after you've simulated to eliminate the seams. It took me less than five minutes to make this pleated section all around the bottom hem. Hope you find it useful! https://youtu.be/OTbwc0_msjA Picot Trim Tutorial below - included the set-up and saving process in Photoshop https://youtu.be/Vo9sjvlmfXg Directions below!! Photoshop Steps 1. Bring Trim image into Photoshop. 2. Crop to a single clean repeat **You will want to leave a little space above and below your trim image. 3. Delete surrounding areas to create negative space and just leave trim parts. 4. Change to greyscale if desired. 4.Export as a transparent PNG. CLO Steps 1. Measure the edges of the pattern where you want to have the trim. 2. Create a rectangle pattern piece matching the length X whatever height you want the trim to be. 3. Create a Fabric and set that fabric to have 0% opacity. 4. Apply the transparent fabric to the rectangle pattern piece created. 5. Place the PNG created onto the fabric to place as a texture image. 6. Scale and re-position the texture image as need on the piece. Enjoy!

post_title: UVs from imported OBJ garment get trashed
post_details: When I import an OBJ as a garment, do some simulation on the avatar, then export the garment as an OBJ or OBJ Sequence, the UVs are completed garbled. How do I preserve the UV mapping that was with the original OBJ when I imported it?

comments.comment_body: Hi, Unfortunately, it's currently not possible to retain the UV mapping. CLO isn't capable of converting OBJs into pattern pieces, which is how a garment draped in CLO generates a UV map. So when you import an OBJ as a garment, the object is in a limbo state and the maps become unusable. Since CLO is intended to be used for physical garment production, where the patterns are created and draped within the software, there is not really a need for UVs to be used as much as in our sister software, Marvelous Designer. I know they've included UV map exporting and editing for their most recent release and I'm sure they are working on this issue of OBJ to Garment conversion. I'm mentioning Marvelous Designer because, depending on your intended use of the software (whether you intend to go into real life production or not), Marvelous may be a more useful software to you. Even though CLO and Marvelous share many features, the motion graphics/FX related functions are added to our new releases much later than on the Marvelous side or sometimes not at all, depending on what users are requesting. (Though hopefully CLO will eventually get the same UV capabilities as Marvelous, since more and more users have recently been requesting it!) In the meantime, I've found some work-arounds for working with OBJs as Garments without the UV map conversion. These are resources created by Marvelous users, but the UI is similar to CLO, so you may be able to try them out even if you are only using CLO currently. Maybe one of the solutions can work with your project. Youtube: OBJ to Garment (using edited OBJ as morph target) Youtube: Marvelous designer / Blender : Object as garment with UV mapping Also try checking the MD Forums. There are some really knowledgeable people on there! I hope this is helpful! Anh

comments.comment_body: Hi! I suggest you two things: 1. Try coordinating the garments with pants unfrozen! 2. Make sure jacket Patterns' right sides are facing up. If the Patterns right side is facing towards the avatar, not towards outside, the Layer option may not work properly. As you see in the image above, although the white pattern has Layer 1, larger value than the pink pattern, pink pattern is placed on top of white pattern since the pink pattern's right side is faced down. To work normally, the pink pattern's right side should face up. After I use the Flip Normal option, facing the pink pattern's right side up, it works perfectly! Tip: Choose Textured Surface icon for Garment Rendering style to check whether right side of Patterns are faced correctly. (https://support.clo3d.com/hc/en-us/articles/115012380508-Garment-Rendering-Style)

post_title: The optimal value of a particle  distance. (PD)
post_details: What is the value of the PD most closely matches the physical properties of the tissue obtained after testing the samples. If the PD is reduced sufficiently strongly, to values less than 5. the physical properties of the tissue change. The fabric becomes softer. Default PD = 20. What is the value of PD to choose the most suitable for the physical properties of the fabric that we tested the samples? According to the developers? Me productivity and speed of simulation does not interest. I have fast enough computer. To me interestingly greatest similar conformity to physical properties of a fabric. Thank you.

comments.comment_body: Dear vadsura, Do you have your physical fabric digitized into CLO using our Fabric Kit? or are you just comparing two similar types of fabric? Depending on the situation, the answer can differ. However, main idea is that you have to use particle distance 5 with Simulate (Complete Nonlinear) option to express fabric realistically. Please keep in mind that we always suggest you to lower the particle distance and apply Complete Nonlinear once all your garment construction is completely finished.

post_title: 6 Things to Know About Particle Distance
post_details: Hi everyone! It's your local CLO designer here. I wanted to make a quick post about an important 3D concept: Particle Distance. I'm sure if you've visited our forums before or tried out the Help Center, you may have come across Particle Distance and not had any idea what anyone was talking about. It can be a very foreign concept, especially if you've never used 3D before. So I'll explain some of the basic stuff about PD below: 1. Particle Distance is the resolution of your 3D pattern pieces. In 3D, every object is made of some kind of polygon mesh. Wikipedia explains it like "A polygon mesh is a collection of vertices, edges and faces that defines the shape of a polyhedral object in 3D computer graphics and solid modeling." But all you have to know as a newbie to 3D and CLO is that a denser mesh = more polygons. And more polygons = more details that can be expressed on that object. The Particle Distance is not the number of polygons in the mesh though! Since each pattern piece will have it's own set of polygons, the Particle Distance is actually the size of each polygon (the length in mm of each polygon's side). So a smaller the Particle Distance = the more polygons in that mesh. Here's what I mean: 2. You can change the PD of your pattern pieces at any time. Yeah, just select a pattern piece with the Transform Pattern tool and find Particle Distance in the Property Editor. If you want to test out PD, open the t-shirt from the library and try to see how much detail is expressed when the PD of the entire garment is at 100 mm versus 5 mm. 3. Yes, things can fall through the mesh too. When you change the t-shirt PD to 100 mm, you'll probably get something like this: So something to keep in mind: if your pattern pieces are falling through the Avatar or each other, it may be because of the Particle Distance. 4. The default PD in CLO is 20 mm. But there are some things to keep in mind........... If a mesh is very dense, more data exists that needs to be calculated by your computer. When things are made with a lot of polygons they tend to slow everything down. Think about early video game characters and CGI movies versus how they look today. Before, game consoles couldn't handle the amount of data it would take to run the kinds of games that exist now. For example: Versus To keep things smooth, all patterns that are imported into CLO or created in CLO have a default PD of 20 mm. It's best to keep most of your pattern pieces at 20 while you're working and still figuring out your design details. Then you can change them near the end or when you need to see a higher level of detail. 5. When you've finalized your design, change the PD of all of your patterns to 5 mm to have the best quality resolution. If you don't want to do this manually, try out the Hi-Res Garment tool. 6. Small pattern pieces should be at 5 mm if you want to see their details. Though we do recommend a working PD of 20, if you have little pieces that are being difficult (collars, bindings, anything smaller than your hand), you can definitely work with them at a PD of 5. Smaller patterns shouldn't affect the simulation speed so much, but test it out and see what works best for you. If you have your own way of explaining Particle Distance or another item to add to my list, comment below and share your wisdom! Anh

comments.comment_body: Thanks, Anh for the explanation. It could be the beginning of a new series " The Topic of The Week" :) So keep doing it. Daniele.

But do not forget that as the PD decreases, the physical properties of the fabric change. I do not recommend using the value of PD = 5 for the animation. First, the simulation will be very long and not always correct. I do not put PD = 5 for animation, only on small details (patterns)

Particle distance does not change the physical properties of fabric. They are 2 different concepts and setting. Particle distance only makes the fabric drape more details. But for animation, it is a good way to not use PD=5 because of the speed.

comments.comment_body: Hi dutchesse1, Unfortunately, there is no way currently to convert pattern pieces into grading information, unless you were able to download a RUL file with the patterns or you created the grading yourself by assigning values to each point. Grading is still a manual process in CLO, so it may be easier to sew up the sizes you need individually instead of grading your pattern. This depends on how comfortable you are with grading and what you need the garments for though. In CLO, if you know the Offset values for a point and that number is consistent for multiple sizes, then you can speed things up by using your arrow keys to move points and lines instead of having to type in each value. For example: 1. I input a number for Arrow Key Movement that matches the Offset value I've calculated for that point. 2. I select the point I want to grade. 3. I hit the right arrow key on my keyboard to move my grading to the right and the bottom arrow key to move the points down. Maybe this will be more efficient than typing in each value, but you may need to do some math to figure out your Offset values.

hey @angelaluna, if exporting and smoothing the avatar in other 3D software is not so feasible, you can subside the issue by increasing the pattern's particle distance to 10.
If you have a particle distance 5 and wrinkles are already formed, try using this trick. Select all, apply 'strengthen'. Turn the simulation on for 1-2 sec.
